sources.title: César Pelli (Q309483), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-24): English label 'César Pelli', description 'Argentine-American architect (1926-2019)', instance of human, born 1926-10-12, died 2019-07-19, citizenship Argentina and the United States, Korean label 시저 펠리. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Cesar Pelli' (read). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Argentine-born architect widely regarded as one of the 20th century's leading designers; worked for Eero Saarinen, was design director at Daniel, Mann, Johnson and Mendenhall (1964-68) and at Gruen Associates (1968-77), perfected glass skins, was dean at Yale (1977-84) and founded Cesar Pelli and Associates (now Pelli Clarke Pelli) in 1977; best known works include the Pacific Design Center, the World Financial Center and Winter Garden, Canary Wharf Tower, Carnegie Hall Tower and the Petronas Twin Towers; AIA Gold Medal 1995. Short reference article, celebratory; its Petronas completion date (1996) differs from obituaries.

Yale School of Architecture, 'Cesar Pelli, 1926-2019' (read in full; institutional obituary with statements from Dean Deborah Berke and Associate Dean Phil Bernstein). As dean he emphasised pedagogical pluralism, revived the student journal Perspecta, founded Retrospecta and an exhibitions programme and redrew the school's shield; later endowed the Cesar Pelli Scholarship Fund (2005) and a landscape architecture professorship (2019). INSTITUTIONAL PRAISE from his own school; used only for dated facts.

Fred A. Bernstein, 'Obituary: César Pelli, 1926-2019', Architectural Record, 21 July 2019 (read in full). Notes he never attained renown as a great form-maker and seemed not to mind; quotes Thomas Hine (New York Times, 1991) that a serious architect working in the commercial arena risks being underestimated and Paul Goldberger on the MoMA expansion's 'bland and dull' exterior; Phil Bernstein on his logical frame of reference; his 1954 move to Saarinen's office, 1964 move to Los Angeles, 1977 Yale deanship and the commissions that followed; his 2018 remark that having a style is a mistake. Professional-magazine obituary with a mild critical edge; credits the 2010 portrait photograph to the Presidencia de la Nacion Argentina.

Metropolis, 'Cesar Pelli obituary' (read in full). Career narrative from Tucuman through Saarinen's office (where he learned to listen to all voices in a firm) to Gruen Associates, the Pacific Design Center, the Yale deanship, Museum Tower and the World Financial Center; testimony from former students and colleagues Jon Pickard and Marion Weiss about how he treated students and employees alike; AIA Gold Medal and Aga Khan Award for the Petronas Towers. Design-press obituary, admiring, drawing on colleagues' recollections.

NPR, 'César Pelli, Renowned Architect Of Skyscrapers Around The World, Dies At 92' (20 July 2019; read in full). Career summary; the MoMA renovation's mixed reviews with Paul Goldberger's remark that it was not avant-garde at all; critic Philip Kennicott on his reconciling generic modernism with a certain loveliness; Petronas Towers as the world's tallest from 1998 to 2004; his 2005 remark that he always looks forward to the next project. General news obituary; relies on quoted critics.

The Architect's Newspaper, 'César Pelli, Argentine architect of the modern skyscraper, dies at age 92' (read in full). Career dates, firm founding, the Pacific Design Center, the World Financial Center and airport terminals, statements from his partner Fred Clarke and the AIA, and the role of his wife, landscape architect Diana Balmori, as a partner on his team. Trade-press obituary built largely on firm and AIA statements.

NBC News, 'Famed architect Cesar Pelli dies at 92' (read in full). Death at his New Haven home confirmed by his firm; his description of architecture as an eminently social art with a deep responsibility toward human beings, history, geography and feelings, quoted from a 2012 magazine interview; reactions from the Argentine president and a client. General news obituary; the one trait quotation is his own.

Vladimir Belogolovsky, 'Everybody Can Share an Opinion, But at The End I'll Decide: In Conversation with Cesar Pelli', ArchDaily (interview recorded January 2005, published 22 July 2019; read in full). SELF-REPORT: his statements that his office tests five or six schemes and 500 to 600 models per project, that he listens to colleagues but makes all decisions himself, that he begins from rational analysis of site, program and climate and distrusts early sketches, that the Petronas Towers were a competition design meant to symbolise a gate to the sky, and that he draws no inspiration from art. Interview by an architecture writer; valuable for process but entirely his own account.

collaboration.rationale: [src_pelli_metropolis, src_pelli_ar, src_pelli_archdaily, src_pelli_archpaper | 1954-2019 | press, press, press interview, press] Metropolis says that in Saarinen's office he learned to listen to every voice in a firm, and former student Marion Weiss and colleague Jon Pickard say he engaged students and employees without distinction; Bernstein says he was beloved by his employees; Pelli himself says he listens to colleagues but decides alone. His wife Diana Balmori worked as a partner on his team (Architect's Newspaper). SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 64 / 0.52 to 62 / 0.50 because the praise comes from former employees and students writing in obituaries and his own interview states he alone decides.

adaptability.rationale: [src_pelli_britannica, src_pelli_ar, src_pelli_metropolis, src_pelli_archdaily | 1952-2019 | reference article, press, press, press interview] He emigrated to the United States in 1952, moved from Saarinen's office to Los Angeles commercial firms in 1964 and to a deanship and his own firm in New Haven in 1977, and Britannica describes his style moving from taut glass skins to stone-clad buildings; in 2018 he said it is a mistake to have a style.

aesthetic_sensitivity.rationale: [src_pelli_ar, src_pelli_britannica, src_pelli_npr | 1975-2012 | press, reference article, press] Obituaries say he focused his creativity on surface treatment (unbroken colour wrappers at the Pacific Design Center, a Mondrian-like facade at Museum Tower), Britannica credits him with perfecting glass skins and crystalline forms, and critic Philip Kennicott speaks of a certain loveliness; these describe the buildings rather than his process. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 70 / 0.56 to 66 / 0.50 because the evidence is critics' description of finished buildings, which firm teams and engineers also shaped.

analytical_rigor.rationale: [src_pelli_ar, src_pelli_archdaily | 1990s-2018 | press, press interview] Phil Bernstein, who worked for him, describes a certain logic and frame of reference behind his design decisions, and in his 2005 interview Pelli says each project begins with rational analysis of site, program, code, wind and climate before any form is considered. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 62 / 0.50 strong inference to 58 / 0.42 inference because one employee's remark and his own account of his process are the only support.

detail_orientation.rationale: [src_pelli_archdaily, src_pelli_ar | 2005 | press interview, press] In 2005 he reported 500 to 600 models per project, including several for a single window design, and Bernstein recalls an understated, measured strategy for articulating a building; the figures are his own and unaudited. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 60 / 0.42 to 58 / 0.40 because the model counts are unverified self-report.

experimentation.rationale: [src_pelli_archdaily | 2005 | press interview] He says his office usually studies five or six schemes and 20 to 30 massing models for a tower. Self-report from a single interview. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 60 / 0.42 to 56 / 0.38 because a single interview is the only source and the models are routine office practice.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_pelli_ar, src_pelli_npr | 1984-2019 | press, press] The evidence is mixed: Architectural Record says he never attained renown as a great form-maker and that some buildings were particularly original and daring, Goldberger found the MoMA expansion not avant-garde at all, and Kennicott credits him with reconciling generic modernism with loveliness; the score stays mid-range.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_pelli_nbc, src_pelli_metropolis, src_pelli_yale | 2005-2019 | press, press, institution] He called architecture an eminently social art with deep responsibility toward human beings (2012), Pickard says he cared most about buildings that give back to the city, and Yale records his scholarship fund (2005) and endowed professorship (2019) for students. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 62 / 0.50 strong inference to 60 / 0.42 inference because the motive is stated mainly in his own interview quotations and a friend's recollection; the scholarship gifts are institutional publicity.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_pelli_ar, src_pelli_npr | 2005-2019 | press, press] He kept working almost until the end of his life although he said he did not need to, and in 2005 said he always looks forward to the next project; evidence is thin and partly his own words.

leadership_drive.rationale: [src_pelli_yale, src_pelli_ar, src_pelli_britannica | 1964-1984 | institution, press, reference article] He became design director at two Los Angeles firms by 1968, was named dean at Yale in 1977, revived Perspecta and founded new school programmes (Yale), and within two months of arriving in New Haven opened his own office to take the MoMA commission (Architectural Record). SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 62 / 0.50 strong inference to 58 / 0.44 inference because the deanship facts come from his school's own obituary and the firm's creation was prompted by a single commission.

portrait.source: Photograph of César Pelli at a presidential audience in the Despacho Presidencial, Casa Rosada, Buenos Aires, 10 June 2010, published in the Presidencia de la Nación Argentina photo gallery (item caption in the holder's 2010 gallery page, read via the Internet Archive snapshot of 15 July 2010: 'La presidenta Cristina Fernández junto al arquitecto César Pelli'). The file is the Wikimedia Commons crop 'César Pelli (cropped).jpg' (811 x 1020) of the 2200 x 1529 original 'Cristina Fernández de Kirchner con César Pelli.jpg'; it is used as is, with no resizing or upscaling and no further crop by this project. Architectural Record's July 2019 obituary independently prints a 2010 photograph of Pelli credited to the Presidencia de la Nación Argentina.
